britannica.rawText:
ANIMAL MAGNETISM.                    329

  ANIMAL MAGNETISM, a pretended power, by which
one person, through certain motions of the hands, is
said to produce extraordinary effects upon the body of
another, and even to cure diseases. It was brought into
notice at Vienna, and afterwards at Paris, by Mesmer,
about the year 1778, whence it is also called Mesmerism.
  In 1784 commissioners appointed by the King of France,
among whom was Dr Franklin, reported that the effects
were owing to the imagination alone, and that the sup-
posed fluid had no existence. Its partisans are never-
theless still numerous in Germany, where it is employed
by some physicians in the treatment of nervous com-
plaints.
  ANIMALCULE, a name given to animals so small as
to be invisible to the naked eye. See Microscope.

passages.text: ANIMAL MAGNETISM, a pretended power, by which one person, through certain motions of the hands, is said to produce extraordinary effects upon the body of another, and even to cure diseases.
It was brought into notice at Vienna, and afterwards at Paris, by Mesmer, about the year 1778, whence it is also called Mesmerism.
In 1784 commissioners appointed by the King of France, among whom was Dr Franklin, reported that the effects were owing to the imagination alone, and that the supposed fluid had no existence.
Its partisans are nevertheless still numerous in Germany, where it is employed by some physicians in the treatment of nervous complaints.
Animal magnetism, also called mesmerism, was a theory put forward by Franz Mesmer in the 18th century that an invisible natural force passes between living things.
A French royal commission in 1784, which included Benjamin Franklin and Antoine Lavoisier, found no evidence of the fluid and attributed the effects to imagination.
The theory is regarded as pseudoscience. Some of its techniques fed into the later practice of hypnosis.
Researchers now attribute the reported effects to suggestion and the placebo effect.

reasons: Same title, but Wikipedia treats animal magnetism as history, not as current medicine.
There is no modern medical article on this subject, so the differences are mostly about framing, not new medical knowledge.
Hypnosis (0.52) and Placebo (0.41) cover what the effects are now thought to be.

suggestedQuestions: Did the 1824 entry believe animal magnetism was real?
What is the modern medical treatment that replaced animal magnetism?

Did the 1824 entry believe animal magnet.answer:
No. It calls animal magnetism "a pretended power" [B1] and reports the 1784 French commission, including Benjamin Franklin, finding the effects due to imagination alone [B3]. Wikipedia gives the same verdict [W2] and calls the theory pseudoscience [W3].

So the scepticism is not new. What changed is the explanation: suggestion and the placebo effect [W4].

What is the modern medical treatment tha.answer: The sources do not support an answer. The 1824 entry mentions use for "nervous complaints" [B4], but the Wikipedia article treats animal magnetism as history and names no treatment that replaced it. Hypnosis is mentioned only as a later practice its techniques fed into [W3].
